title: Terminal, Console & TTY
summary: A terminal emulator is a graphical text interface that passes user keystrokes to a shell and renders text stream outputs according to ANSI escape codes.

body.definition: A software application that emulates the behavior of physical tele-typewriter (TTY) video terminals (such as the DEC VT100) inside a graphical window system.

body.text: In early mainframe computing, terminals were physical electromechanical hardware units connected over serial cables. Modern Linux systems emulate this architecture through pseudo-terminals (pty), which pair a master process (the GUI terminal window) with a slave device that standard Unix command-line utilities interact with.
Standard I/O File Descriptors

items: stdin (File Descriptor 0): The standard input text stream (keyboard keystrokes or piped input).
stdout (File Descriptor 1): The standard output stream for normal program results.
stderr (File Descriptor 2): The dedicated unbuffered error diagnostic stream.

body.text: ANSI escape sequences (e.g. `\033[31m`) allow command-line tools to control cursor position, text styling, and 24-bit RGB colors in terminal emulators.

title: sudo & Privilege Escalation
summary: The sudo command allows permitted users to execute commands with root superuser privileges while preserving an audited security trail.

body.definition: A Unix security program that allows a designated user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, governed by rules configured in `/etc/sudoers`.

body.text: Logging in directly as the root superuser is dangerous because a single typo can wipe system partitions. Using `sudo` follows the Principle of Least Privilege: users operate under standard unprivileged accounts for daily tasks and temporarily elevate only specific administrative commands.
Key Security Features of sudo

items: Granular Permission Control: Admins can restrict specific users to run only certain commands (e.g. restart web server) without full root access.
Syslog Auditing: Every execution of sudo is timestamped and logged to `/var/log/auth.log` or systemd journal.
Password Timestamp Caching: Caches authorization for 5 to 15 minutes to prevent repetitive password prompts.

body.text: Always edit the sudoers configuration file with `visudo` to perform syntax validation before saving, preventing accidental system lockouts.

title: Unix File Permissions & Ownership
summary: Unix file permissions enforce security across User, Group, and Others through Read, Write, and Execute bit masks stored in filesystem inodes.

body.definition: A 9-bit security mode stored in a file's inode that controls read (r), write (w), and execute (x) access for owner, group, and world scopes.

body.text: When running `ls -l`, permissions appear as a 10-character string like `-rwxr-xr--`. The first character denotes file type (`-` for regular file, `d` for directory). The remaining nine characters are broken into three triplets: User/Owner, Group, and Others.
Permission Modes Explained

rows.label: w (Write)
values: Create, rename, or delete files inside directory

rows.label: x (Execute)
values: Traverse into directory (`cd`) and access files inside

body.text: A user must have execute (x) permission on a directory to enter it or access any file stored within it, even if they have read access on the file itself.

relatedLinks.label: Arch Wiki — File permissions and attributes

title: chmod & Numeric Octal Modes
summary: The chmod command alters filesystem permission bits using symbolic syntax or 3-digit octal notation like 755, 644, and 700.

body.definition: A standard POSIX system utility and system call used to modify the access permission flags of filesystem objects.

body.text: Numeric octal notation sums permission values (Read=4, Write=2, Execute=1) for each tier. For example, `chmod 755 script.sh` sets `7` (4+2+1, rwx) for the owner, `5` (4+0+1, r-x) for the group, and `5` (r-x) for all others.
Common Standard Octal Configurations

items: 644 (`-rw-r--r--`): Default for public web assets and configuration files (owner can edit; everyone can read).
755 (`-rwxr-xr-x`): Standard for executable binaries and accessible directories.
700 (`-rwx------`): Private scripts or directories (e.g. `~/.ssh`) restricted exclusively to the owner.
600 (`-rw-------`): Private cryptographic keys (e.g. `id_ed25519`) unreadable by any other user.

body.text: Special permission bits include SUID (4000), SGID (2000), and the Sticky Bit (1000, used on `/tmp` so users cannot delete each other's files).

title: SSH (Secure Shell Protocol)
summary: SSH provides an encrypted cryptographic network tunnel on TCP port 22 for secure remote terminal access and automated file transfers.

body.definition: A cryptographic network protocol that operates on a client-server model over untrusted networks to provide authenticated, encrypted terminal sessions.

body.text: SSH replaced legacy unencrypted protocols like Telnet and rlogin, which transmitted passwords in cleartext. SSH uses asymmetric public-key cryptography (such as Ed25519 or RSA) for authentication, then negotiates a symmetric cipher (ChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM) to encrypt all ongoing session traffic.
Core SSH Capabilities

items: Public-Key Authentication: Logging in with a private key file without typing interactive passwords.
Local & Remote Port Forwarding: Securely tunneling remote databases or web interfaces through encrypted SSH tunnels.
SFTP / SCP Integration: Encrypted file management and file synchronization.

body.text: Modern best practices mandate using modern elliptic curve keys (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`) and disabling password authentication in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`.

title: Linux Package Managers Explained
summary: Package managers automate installing, updating, and resolving dependency graphs for software packages from signed, trusted repositories.

body.definition: A collection of software tools and metadata formats that automates downloading, verifying GPG signatures, resolving library dependencies, and installing binaries onto the root filesystem.

body.text: Instead of hunting for `.exe` installers across untrusted websites, Linux users retrieve verified software from centralized distribution mirrors. The package manager inspects the dependency graph, installs any required shared `.so` libraries, unpacks binaries, and configures system services automatically.
Package Manager Tasks

items: Dependency Resolution: Solves mathematical Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problems to guarantee all required runtime libraries are compatible.
Cryptographic Verification: Verifies GPG signatures to ensure packages have not been tampered with in transit.
Atomic File Tracking: Maintains a local database of every installed file so uninstallation cleanly removes every orphaned trace.

body.text: Modern universal sandbox packaging formats like Flatpak and Snap package dependencies internally to run across any Linux distribution.

title: APT vs Pacman vs DNF
summary: Different Linux distro families use distinct package managers: Debian/Ubuntu uses APT, Arch Linux uses Pacman, and Fedora/RHEL uses DNF.

body.definition: Binary archive standards (`.deb`, `.rpm`, `.pkg.tar.zst`) containing pre-compiled binaries, file metadata, and installation lifecycle trigger scripts.

body.text: While all three managers perform the same fundamental tasks, their syntax, release philosophies, and speed differ. Pacman on Arch Linux is rolling-release and lightweight; APT on Ubuntu focuses on rock-solid point-release stability; DNF on Fedora features advanced libsolv SAT solving.
Command Equivalents
DNF5 is a rewrite in C++ that dramatically reduces metadata download times and memory consumption compared to legacy Python DNF.

title: The Root User (UID 0)
summary: Root is the all-powerful superuser account with User ID (UID) 0 that bypasses all standard filesystem permission checks on Unix systems.

body.definition: The default administrative account in Unix-like operating systems with unrestricted access to all kernel resources, hardware devices, and system calls.

body.text: In Unix design philosophy, the root user is completely omnipotent. The Linux kernel will not prevent root from deleting vital system directories, overwriting raw disk blocks (`/dev/sda`), or killing critical init daemons. Modern Linux distributions mitigate this using Linux Capabilities and SELinux/AppArmor Mandatory Access Controls (MAC).
Root vs Linux Capabilities

items: `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`: Privilege to bind network sockets below port 1024 without full root access.
`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`: Overarching system administration capability encompassing disk mounting and kernel tracing.
`CAP_CHOWN`: Permission to arbitrarily change file ownership.

body.text: Splitting root privileges into fine-grained capabilities allows services (like web servers or ping) to execute securely with minimal attack surfaces.

title: Shells: Bash, Zsh & POSIX
summary: A shell is a command language interpreter that reads interactive user commands or scripts and executes them by making kernel system calls.

body.definition: A command-line interpreter program that acts as an interface between the user and the operating system kernel, supporting scripting logic, piping, and job control.

body.text: When you type a command in a terminal, the shell parses the syntax, expands environment variables, manages I/O redirection, searches the `$PATH` directory list for matching executable binaries, and forks a child process to execute the binary.
Popular Shells Compared

items: Bash (Bourne Again Shell): The ubiquitous default shell across Linux distributions for the last 30 years.
Zsh (Z Shell): Modern interactive shell with advanced autocomplete, syntax highlighting, and theme frameworks (default on macOS).
Fish (Friendly Interactive Shell): Out-of-the-box autosuggestions and web configuration without complex script setup.

body.text: The Unix pipe operator (`|`) streams the stdout of one program directly into the stdin of another without creating intermediate temporary disk files.

title: Cron Jobs & Scheduled Tasks
summary: Cron is a background daemon that executes recurring automated scripts and maintenance tasks on schedules defined by 5-field crontab syntax.

body.definition: A time-based job scheduler in Unix-like operating systems that runs in the background, waking every minute to execute scheduled batch commands.

body.text: Cron schedules are maintained in user crontab files (`crontab -e`). System administrators rely on cron for database backups, log rotation, security scans, and periodic cleanup scripts without manual intervention.
Crontab 5-Field Syntax

items: Minute (0 - 59)
Hour (0 - 23)
Day of the Month (1 - 31)
Month (1 - 12)
Day of the Week (0 - 6, where 0 = Sunday)

body.text: Systemd Timers (`.timer` units) are increasingly used as modern alternatives to cron, offering millisecond precision, dependency chaining, and persistent catch-up logging.
